title: How long will you wait?
hook: you're not a child anymore, and Socrates became himself by attending to reason in everything (Enchiridion 51)

segments.voice: Yesterday: Chrysippus, the explainers, and the one line you actually live. Your line was live the book. Which line did you live? Day three hundred eighty-five.

Monday. That's when it starts. Or the first of the month. Or after the holidays, after this project, after the kids are older, after things calm down. Almost everyone has a thing they're going to begin, and a date it's going to begin on, and the date keeps moving. Near the very end of the handbook, Epictetus stops giving rules and turns to his student with a question. It's the sharpest sentence in the book, and it's aimed straight at that moving date. Today: how long will you wait?
screen: `MONDAY. THE FIRST OF THE MONTH.` → `THE DATE KEEPS MOVING.` → `HOW LONG WILL YOU WAIT?`

segments.voice: First, the question. How long will you put off thinking yourself worthy of the best things, Epictetus asks, and never crossing what reason tells you? You've received the principles you ought to accept. You've accepted them. So what teacher are you still waiting for, before you start setting yourself right? Second, the plain fact. You're not a boy any longer, he says. You're a grown adult. If you keep being careless and lazy, adding delay to delay, setting one day and then another for when you'll start paying attention to yourself, you'll fail to notice you're not making progress, and you'll live and die an ordinary person. Third, the games. Whenever something hard or pleasant, or glorious or shameful, comes along, he says, remember: the contest is now. The Olympic games are here. They can't be put off. Progress is saved or lost by a single day, a single giving way. The Greek word for contest is agōn, the root of our word agony. It meant the struggle of the games before it meant pain. Fourth, Socrates. This is how Socrates became who he was, Epictetus says: by paying attention to nothing but reason in everything he met. And you, even if you're not yet Socrates, should live as someone who wants to be. And a look back at the week, since today closes it: doesn't follow. Quickly, not badly. Show the wool. In secret. Blame no one. Live the book. Each of them could start today.
screen: `WHAT TEACHER ARE YOU WAITING FOR?` · `NOT A BOY ANY LONGER.` · `THE CONTEST IS NOW.` · `LIVE AS ONE WHO WANTS TO BE SOCRATES.` · then, large: `HOW LONG WILL YOU WAIT?`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Name the thing you've been meaning to start. The call, the practice, the apology, the application, the first page. Notice the date you've been giving it: Monday, next month, someday. Now ask Epictetus' question, kindly but honestly: how long will you wait? Then find the smallest first step that could happen today, small enough that there's no reason to postpone it. Picture taking it. The bell holds the time.
How long will you wait? Epictetus' question near the handbook's end: you're grown, the contest is now, and the games can't be put off. Today's word.
screen: `HOW LONG WILL YOU WAIT? — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: how long will you wait. Start the thing today, even if it's only the smallest first step. Day three hundred eighty-five.

howItsDone: Many people practicing Stoicism return to Enchiridion 51 when they notice themselves postponing something important, and take one small step that same day.

original.note: Greek: a contest or struggle, the root of English agony. In Enchiridion 51, the contest is now.

trapdoor: what it means: you're grown and already have the principles; the contest is today, and no teacher is coming to start it for you.
what a scholar hears: agōn, the Olympic contest; Epictetus holds up Socrates, who attended to nothing but reason, as the model.

notes: Enchiridion 51 paraphrased: how long will you delay to think yourself worthy of the best things; you have received the principles; what teacher do you wait for; you are no longer a youth but a full-grown man; if negligent and slothful you will live and die an ordinary man; the contest is now, the Olympic games are here; progress is lost or saved by one defeat and one giving way; Socrates became perfect by attending to nothing but reason; live as one who wishes to be Socrates.
